paper.title: Glutamate/GABA Resource Asymmetry Enables Bidirectional Activity Correction
paper.abstract: Glutamate/GABA cotransmission allows one neuron to excite and inhibit the same target. How the two release branches translate a shared spike train into net synaptic drive, and how this drive shapes neural circuit activity, remain unclear. We introduce BRIDGE, a model with separate glutamate and GABA resources that deplete and recover under shared input. The model reproduced glutamatergic depression during repeated stimulation in cotransmission recordings. Late GABAergic responses showed weaker frequency dependence. This asymmetry can generate negative differential gain in the model, allowing faster presynaptic firing to weaken net drive while output remains excitatory. In simulated circuits, cotransmitting neurons shifted their output toward excitation when activity fell and toward inhibition when it rose, improving recovery after perturbations across all circuit sizes tested. Compared with baseline, a simplified spiking implementation yielded higher mean accuracy in most classification comparisons and lower error in selected prediction tasks. Thus, resource asymmetry links firing history to bidirectional correction of circuit activity.

paper.title: Disentangling tonic and phasic dopamine in fiber photometry from single recordings to cohorts
paper.abstract: Fiber photometry signals combine fast neurotransmitter transients with slower changes in baseline. However, current pipelines separate the two before measuring either, so errors in one carry over into the other. Here we present PhotoSVI, a multi-scale statistical model that splits a recording into a slow tonic signal and discrete release events, estimated together. For each recording, PhotoSVI returns event probabilities over time, the drug effect on event rate with its uncertainty, and the time course of the tonic response, and it pools recordings across a cohort. In simulations matched to experimental recordings, PhotoSVI detected transients and recovered the shape of the tonic response more accurately than existing methods. In mouse dopamine recordings, it revealed an effect that count-based analyses largely missed: a nociceptin receptor agonist enhances the phasic response to morphine while reducing the tonic one, consistent with lower tonic dopamine relieving phasic release from autoreceptor inhibition.

paper.title: PreSMA population dynamics keep the beat atop the primate audiomotor hierarchy
paper.abstract: Humans move in time with musical beats, yet how the brain builds the internal beat that guides movement is unknown. We recorded 4,719 neurons in six nodes of the audiomotor circuit while monkeys tapped in synchrony with auditory metronomes at different tempos. We found a clear functional dissociation in the temporal-frontal axis. Auditory cortex detected metronome clicks and contained local clocks that tiled each interstimulus interval, whereas parietal, striatal, and motor areas, most strongly the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA), generated movement-aligned neural sequences that rescaled with tempo. Only in preSMA did population activity formed a cone-shaped manifold that jointly encoded tempo in its height, the produced interval in its width, and the timing of each tap relative to the beat in its position along the trajectory. During timing errors, preSMA activity kept conical shape but drifted toward shorter or longer tempos, revealing a hierarchical neural clock for beat synchronization.

paper.title: Fully Spiking Neural Implementation of Lambda-Calculus Beta-Reduction via Biologically Documented Mechanisms
paper.abstract: We present the first complete implementation of $\beta$-reduction in the untyped $\lambda$-calculus using exclusively spiking neural dynamics. Every step of the reduction---redex detection, subterm segmentation, variable-binding detection, De~Bruijn index arithmetic, token copying, and inter-step role maintenance---is performed by leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with explicit membrane dynamics, exponential synaptic currents, axonal delays, and pair-based spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP). Each neural component maps onto a specific, experimentally documented mechanism: Jeffress-type delay-line coincidence for redex detection; a line-attractor balance counter for subterm segmentation; $\theta$--$\gamma$ cross-frequency coupling for De~Bruijn variable binding; a phase-ring traveling wave for depth-index arithmetic; theta-cycle STDP for token copying; and recurrent persistent firing for role maintenance between reduction steps. All synaptic weights are derived analytically from measured EPSP amplitudes; no hand tuning is performed. The closed-loop system achieves 100\,\% agreement with a symbolic oracle across ten validation classes, including Church numeral arithmetic (\textsc{plus}, \textsc{mult}, \textsc{pred}), Boolean logic with divergent branches, Y-combinator steps, terms with up to six bound-variable occurrences, De~Bruijn indices up to~12, noise robustness, and determinism. To our knowledge this is the first Turing-complete symbolic computation performed entirely within spike dynamics using biologically grounded circuit primitives. We discuss implications for neuromorphic proof assistants and the neural basis of symbolic reasoning.
